## gm pass, Phase B completed: run_code compiles for wasm32-wasi, and the Chromium witness runs (2026-11-10)

Compile. The engine's blockers were the C++ facilities that the WASI libc++ here does not provide: std::mutex, std::shared_mutex, std::this_thread, std::ifstream and the std::filesystem directory and stat operations. std::filesystem::path itself compiles for wasi. The fix is at the cause, one platform layer for the two OS facilities the engine uses: native/components/quickjs/platform.hpp and platform.cpp. Native keeps std::filesystem, std::ifstream and the std mutex types. WASI uses stdio, POSIX stat, opendir and nanosleep, and single-threaded no-op locks (WASI here has no threads). engine.cpp, runcode.cpp and leaves.cpp call platform:: and no longer include the std headers for those facilities. platform.cpp is added to gm_runcode.

The Threads error was a second cause. The root CMakeLists linked Threads::Threads into deoxidene for every platform, and wasi-libc here has no pthread library, so the reactor link failed with `unable to find dynamic system library "pthreads"`. On WASI, Threads::Threads is now an empty interface target; the mcp and mcpclient find_package calls are gone (the root call runs first). This is why the earlier quickjs-only conditional was reverted.

Link. gm_txiki_wasi links gm_runcode, gm_txiki_core_wasi, gm_json and gm_quickjs_ng again. Build: `cmake --build build/wasi --target gm_txiki_wasi -j 8`, foreground, timeout 900 s, exit 0. Caveat, measured below: a static archive member is linked only when something references it, and no export reaches the engine, so the reactor contains no engine code. The sizes did not change. A body-run export is a new surface and needs the owner's decision.

## gm pass, Phase B: run_code and its 120 s deadline in the wasm32-wasi reactor (2026-11-10)

Build fixes, each at its cause (the wasi toolchain here is zig 0.17.1 with its wasi libc++ and libc++abi):
- Exceptions. The wasi libc++abi has no exception runtime (__cxa_throw and friends are undefined), the same reason thebird compiles ada with -fno-exceptions. Root CMakeLists.txt adds -fno-exceptions to C++ and -g0 to every wasi compile. The four C++ try sites in engine.cpp (call_host, host_names), leaves.cpp (log_refusal) and runcode.cpp (call_verb) compile only when __cpp_exceptions is defined; the wasi build runs the same bodies without the catch, and no wasi verb or host can throw.
- Thread-local destructors. thread_body_controls in native/include/gm/runcode.hpp is a plain static on __wasi__: wasi libc++abi has no __cxa_thread_atexit, and the reactor has one thread.
- Path library. Zig's wasi libc++ lacks the out-of-line std::filesystem::path members (lexically_normal, __root_directory, __filename). Two uses reach the reactor: the project package.json join and the ESM specifier normalizer. platform.hpp gains join_path and normal_path: native uses / and lexically_normal (unchanged behaviour); wasi joins strings and normalizes segments (a '..' above the root is dropped for an absolute path).
- Witness code. The browser page compiles the module synchronously (XMLHttpRequest with x-user-defined), because the page's dump is taken at load and Chromium's async compile is not waited on. Chromium refuses a synchronous compile above 8 MB on the main thread; -g0 brings the reactor under it (raw 5176695, from 12048363). --enable-features=WebAssemblyUnlimitedSyncCompilation was tried first and had no effect: /etc/chromium.d/90-gpu appends its own --enable-features, which wins.
- poll_oneoff. The page's shim waits for clock subscriptions by busy-waiting on performance.now and reports the expired ones; the Node witness uses node:wasi.

Cause: leaves_dir_of preferred any leaves/ directory beside the binary, and build/release/native/components/host/leaves is a copy dated 05:13 that a build does not refresh; it had no git_state. skills_dir_of already prefers the checkout (2026-11-10). 5. The gate's skills check failed on three rule lines that named run_shell, grep and git_status without the gm. prefix. Fix: the prefix, then the gate passed on 472aaec.
6. Witness only, not a product defect: the check's workspace counted gm's own runs/ directory as untracked. The check's .gitignore now lists .gm/ and runs/. git_state reports runs/ correctly when a project does not ignore it.

## gm pass, Phase A (2026-11-10): installed-build update prepared, not installed

Owner instruction (pasted queue, 2026-11-10): prepare the installed-build update as Phase A only: code, docs and tests, committed locally, nothing pushed, no install. The install touches every peer, so it waits until no peer is busy.

Changes:

1. Served-skill freshness on an old connection. Cause: resources/read of a skill returned ttlMs 3600000 with cacheScope public, so a client holding a connection that started before an update kept the old skill text for up to an hour, and the new skill was not served on that connection. Change: the skill read is volatile (ttlMs 0) on both engines. native/components/mcp/server.cpp read_resource uses kVolatileTtlMs; src/mcp.mjs readResource uses VOLATILE_TTL_MS. The reader itself already re-reads the file on each call (SkillCache::get, skillOf), so the stale part was the cache hint.
   Witness (Phase B, after the install): node tools/check-installed-build.mjs /config/.gmnew/current/gm <sha> asserts resources/read of skill://gm/SKILL.md has ttlMs 0 and equals the binary's skills copy. Before the install the installed build returns ttlMs 3600000, so the check fails there, which is the defect it measures.

2. fcb84df task-leak install rows, as exact install steps. Cause: the installed gm 78ca5a1 predates fcb84df (a non-owner task replacement is refused after the first step) and 70e4349 (the updater finds gmnew-<target>). Steps, in order:
   a. Check that no peer is busy: ListAgents shows no peer as busy. At 08:4x fx-e1 was busy, so this step waits.
   b. Check that the published release carries the fixes: scripts/install.sh fetches manifest.json from GMNEW_RELEASE_BASE (default https://github.com/AnEntrypoint/gm/releases/download/latest). Run curl -fsSL that URL and read the version. Proceed only when the version is the release cut from a main commit at or after this pass (the fcb84df, 70e4349 and the change 1 commit). If it is older, the install would put back the old build: wait for the release.
   c. Run sh scripts/install.sh. It verifies sha256 and size from the manifest, stages the archive, and keeps the previous install in ~/.gmnew/previous.<pid>.
   d. Run node tools/check-installed-build.mjs /config/.gmnew/current/gm <release sha> (change 3 below). Expect installed-build-check: ok.
   e. Peers reload on a binary change (native peers reload on a leaf, skill or binary change), so no peer restarts by hand. Re-read the task-leak refusal with a non-owner next_context task replacement after one step; it must be refused.
   Witness: the step d output, and the step e refusal text quoted from the run log.

3. A check that runs the installed build's version and skill serve: tools/check-installed-build.mjs (new). Usage: node tools/check-installed-build.mjs <installed gm> [expected stamp prefix]. It runs <binary> --version, opens serve on a scratch workspace with playwriter disabled, reads initialize serverInfo.version, reads skill://gm/SKILL.md, and requires the text to equal <binary dir>/skills/gm/SKILL.md and ttlMs 0. Witness (Phase B): run it on /config/.gmnew/current/gm after step 2c; it must print installed-build-check: ok. Before the install it fails on ttlMs and on the skill text, which is the point.

Gap: the time from an assistant record's end to the next user prompt. It mixes the user's time away with time a job spent running after the turn ended, so it does not isolate the waste.

gm run logs (/workspace/gm/runs, 444 runs, 9346 actions):

- 1699 actions repeat an earlier action in the same run (same tool and arguments). By tool: child_context 768, next_context 367, run_shell 297, run_code 185, write_file 48, edit_file 11, others under 10.
- Run 2026-11-05-19-07-15-bce32b: 472 repeated actions. Its top call is child_context with the child and run arguments, 264 times, with no wait. That is a polling loop.
- Run 2026-11-05-15-30-50-484992: 393 repeated actions.
- skill-loaded events: 157 across the 444 runs.
- next_context with a waitMs argument: 1 in the run logs. The transcripts show the wait form is used (14 to 18 times per session), so the run logs and the transcripts count different things; the transcript count is the measured wait use.

Three waste sources, each with the habit that addresses it (skills/gm/SKILL.md, Habits):

1. Zero-wait polling (child_context 264 times in one run, next_context repeated across runs): habit "Wait in one call, do not poll".
2. Repeated skill reads (13 in session 7ae15e26; 157 skill-loaded events): habit "Read the served skill once per connection".
3. Turns that end while their own job runs (median gap 117 to 508 s, p90 222 to 1588 s across the three sessions, which mix user time with job time): habit "Keep the wait in the turn that started the job".

Not addressed by a new habit: the 2562 tool uses and 623 KB of results over 20000 characters in session 7ae15e26. The existing habit "Keep what you carry small" covers them; the measured repeat is in the next line.

Input: thebird origin/main at 6faf4c5 (pin scripts/txiki/pin.json, tjsWasmSha256 f716451387bd721e1b0cede84cc5ab44b10c6087e16dde78e206e12e70b1f296). /workspace/thebird/web/vendor/txiki/tjs.wasm is untracked there; its sha256 is f716451387bd721e1b0cede84cc5ab44b10c6087e16dde78e206e12e70b1f296, the pinned value. gm ran it through txiki/node.mjs against the four probe files of thebird's scripts/witness.mjs (lines 363 to 366), staged in /tmp/gm-import-probe (scratch, removed by nothing; outside the checkout).

Defects found by the first run, both in gm's own txiki runner, fixed in 916aefe:

1. The runner called tjs_browser_eval with the code pointer only. thebird's entry takes a second argument, the module label (its web runner passes it, txiki-in-page.js callEval). Without it relative imports had no base: script-imports failed with "Uncaught ReferenceError: could not load 'm.mjs'", and eval-import printed nothing. Fix: txiki/host.mjs run() takes name (the entry's absolute project path) and passes it as the label; txiki/node.mjs and txiki/site.mjs pass the entry name.

Fix: txiki/fs.mjs implements tjs_fs_realpath against the project (the path when project.stat finds it, else -1). tjs_fs_rename remains stubbed; no probe uses it.

## Fixed cost of a gm call and the process wait (2026-11-11, Phase A, item 7)

- Measured with tools/measure-call-cost.mjs (native, 40 calls each, medians): trivial run_code 8.7 ms, reply 336 bytes; next_context with nothing new 1.0 ms, 331 bytes; next_context full 17.4 ms, about 4.7 KB; the full reply's largest fields are rules 758 bytes, events 553, witness 138, pendingCommands 139, query 104. Node: 31.9 ms, 0.2 ms, 0.7 ms.
- Conclusion from the measurement: the wall-time fixed cost per call is milliseconds, and the full reply is paid once per run, so no change to next_context or run_code startup. Their cost in turns is the peers' cost, not their wall time.
- gm.job_status({ pid, waitMs }) returns on exit: a 2 s process returned at 2.01 s (median of 3) and a 4 s process at 4.03 s with waitMs 1000 in a loop.
- Change: skills/gm/SKILL.md, two job-wait habits, now say a longer wait is one run_code body that loops job_status until the state is not running (the loop is in the skill text, with the measured numbers). Wall time of the change: the loop body returned at 4.03 s for a 4 s process; no code change in either engine, no new verb.
- Witness: tools/measure-call-cost.mjs build/release/native/components/host/gm 5 (prints the looped-wait line for a 60 s process; the reply arrives at about 60.1 s in one call).

## The clock knob is guarded, and the progress interval is on the clock (2026-11-11, Phase A)

- Where it is read: native/include/gm/clock.hpp, clock_scale(), once, on first use. It is honoured only when GMNEW_TEST_CLOCK is exactly "1" and GM_CLOCK_SCALE parses to a value in (0, 1]; anything else is 1. Node: the CLOCK_SCALE lines in src/mcp.mjs and src/tools.mjs use the same rule.
- A peer's environment with GM_CLOCK_SCALE alone changes nothing; a peer would need both variables, and the only things that set GMNEW_TEST_CLOCK are the checks. The scale can only shorten, so the flag gate is the only way a real run's timers move.
- native/components/mcp/server.cpp: the run_code progress notice interval (kProgressMs, 5000 ms) is multiplied by clock_scale() in the wait.
- tools/check-run-code-progress.mjs: scaled like the other two (body 117 ms, 33 ms budget, 500 ms budget). Measured: ok in 0.40 s, one progress notice (was 13.3 s).
- check-browser-scope is not on the clock: its 12.7 s is browser work in external processes (the playwriter browser start and close), not a timer. Not changed.

## Mutation check for the scaled budgets (2026-11-11, Phase A)

- native/components/host/worker.cpp: the --job-lifetime-ms value (and the default) is multiplied by clock_scale(), so the JS body budget moves with GM_CLOCK_SCALE under the test flag. The guard is the same as for the other two knobs.
- tools/check-clock-mutations.mjs (new): a guard run (a 2000 ms body with no timeoutMs must stay foreground when GM_CLOCK_SCALE is set without GMNEW_TEST_CLOCK), then two mutants, each applied to the source, built, run against its scaled check (which must fail), and reverted, with a rebuild after: the job lifetime back to 60 s (check-run-code-budget.mjs) and the job wait cap back to 30 s (check-turn-economy.mjs). Measured: both mutants fail with exit 1; the guard passes; wall 122.2 s (two mutant builds and the restore).
- tools/check-build.mjs: `--mutations` adds the mutation check as an exclusive scenario (never cached, outside the default set).

Bound choice: 6000 keeps 154 of 202 run_shell results from 2026-11-11 whole, and saves 189,031 of 782,375 characters.
- Phase A: an identical read_file call in the same run, with no write verb (write_file, edit_file, fs_op, run_shell) between, is answered with a pointer to its step (body_call in server.cpp); fresh: true reads again. run_shell is not repeated this way, because a shell command can change state the run cannot see.

## Round e6b5, macOS x64 turn-economy and build-handover: the races (Phase A)

Run 43120046392 on f43b25f: macOS x64 failed two checks, arm64 passed. Causes, and the fixes (no check budget was loosened):

- check-turn-economy, "job_status did not return the slow job's exit": job_status clamps waitMs to 60000 * clock_scale(), which is 1000 ms under the test clock. The slow job sleeps 750 ms plus shell start-up, so on x64 it exited just after the clamp expired, and the reply read the status file before the settle. Change: a job_status wait is capped at the real 60000 ms (job_wait_ceiling_ms in verbs/job.cpp) and returns when the job settles; the pid wait keeps the scaled clamp. Witness on Linux: check-turn-economy ok.
- check-build-handover, "the worker should run ... once the shell call finished": after the 35 s shell call the check slept 400 ms (4000 * 0.1) and read the worker's exe once, but the handover to the new build takes longer on x64. Change: the check polls the worker's exe until it runs the new build, bounded by the shell call's own timeoutMs (120000 at the same scale). Witness on Linux: check-build-handover ok.
- Witness on macOS: the next release run, both x64 and arm64.
- native/components/tool/ship.cpp (ship --push): the upstream phase-b marker stays required at HEAD; the push also refuses unless origin main is an ancestor of HEAD, waits for release and arm-diagnose to succeed on HEAD (gh run list --commit), rechecks origin, then pushes main. Witness: the candidate release build compiles ship.cpp; the first real push by this path is the next green candidate.
- native/components/host/include/gm/host/relay.hpp (handshake_timeout back to 10000 ms from 90000, the d5c65b1 value): check-relay-reexec failed on release 43124120966 (31ee1ca) and 43129838013 (ab5614a), both with the 90 s budget, with "the relay re-executed only after the next_context wait had answered"; it passed on release 43122134796 (c836de6, 10 s). The mechanism is not proven; this revert is the A/B. Witness: the next candidate release run passes check-relay-reexec.

## Round x64 macOS check-worker-growth: cause and measurement fix (2026-11-12)

- Measured on Linux release: 400 calls grew 352 KB (earlier single window); 4000 calls grew 396 KB. So the release worker keeps no per-call memory; the early 352 KB was allocator growth. A single window of 400 calls therefore counts one-time allocator growth as worker growth.
- macOS: the check reads ps -o rss=, which reports KB on macOS and is the same process (worker_pid finds the gm-core descendant by exe). The macOS single-window growth of 2.8 to 3.6 MB is the same kind of measurement, and on macOS libmalloc grows the heap in steps that a single window of 400 calls can cross. Whether macOS also retains per call is not shown by any run here (no macOS host).
- Measurement fix (native/components/tool/checks/worker_growth.cpp): the check first runs 400 calls (allocator warm-up), then measures RSS before and after a second 400 calls. The limit (2048 KB) is unchanged and applies to the second window. Per-call retention shows up in the second window; one-time growth does not.
- Witness, Linux release: check-worker-growth: ok (... over the second 400 run_code calls, after 400 more and 100 warm calls (growth -16 KB; wall 6.4 s)).
- Open, ASan only: the same check on build/asan with the quarantine disabled still grows 3400 KB over the second window (58636 KB then 62036 KB), so the ASan residual is per-call retention of about 8.5 KB per call. It is absent in the release build and the asan job excludes this check. Cause not established (ASan allocator metadata or a real retention that only ASan's allocator exposes).
- Open, macOS: the next release run decides it. If macOS's second window stays near 3 MB, macOS retains per call, and that is a product defect to investigate in the worker. If the second window is near 0, the first window was allocator warm-up.

## Round item 3: LeakSanitizer on the ASan worker, 8.5 KB per call (2026-11-12)

- Method (scratch driver in /tmp, not in the repo): the ASan relay (build/asan gm serve, the check's argv) driven over stdio with 100 warm-up and 400 to 500 run_code calls ("return 1;"), then stdin closed so the worker exits on its own. The worker's stderr is the driver's file (checked through /proc fd 2). The worker's LeakSanitizer runs at its exit: verbosity=1 prints "LeakSanitizer: checking for leaks" from the worker process, and with detect_leaks=1 the 500-call run printed no "detected memory leaks" report.

The release build measured 4000 calls with 396 KB growth (no per-call growth), so this is an ASan-build effect that the release build does not show.

## Round stretch-end enforcement: gm-tool repos (2026-11-12)

- Design: `gm-tool repos` lists six repos (gm, fx, jayzee, thebird, hy4-relay, hyperagent) with uncommitted files (git status --porcelain) and commits ahead of the upstream (rev-list @{u}..HEAD). A repo with no upstream is reported as blocked. Report mode exits 0; `--strict` exits 1 when gm itself is not clean and pushed.
- Scope decision: the Phase B step does not commit or push peers' work. Their uncommitted changes and ahead commits belong to their owners, and the owner rules forbid committing another session's work under lanmower. The step reports each peer with its cause (uncommitted count, ahead count, or no upstream); gm's own work is committed with ship and pushed through its Phase B.
- Files: native/components/tool/repos.cpp (new; repos_command), native/include/gm/tool.hpp (declaration), native/components/tool/main.cpp (dispatch of `repos`), native/components/tool/CMakeLists.txt (repos.cpp in gm_tool_checks), skills/dev/SKILL.md (end-of-stretch rule in the commit section).
- Witness at the time of writing (report mode): gm 4 uncommitted (this round's files); fx absent from this tree; jayzee 0 uncommitted, 8 ahead; thebird 0 uncommitted, 1 ahead; hy4-relay 16 uncommitted, no upstream; hyperagent 1 uncommitted. `--strict` exits 1 while gm is not clean and pushed.
- Not covered: fx is not a checkout in this tree, so its state is reported as absent; a repo elsewhere needs its path added to the list.

## Round stretch-end scope change: gm checks only its own repo (2026-11-12)

- Requirement change: gm-tool repos checks only the repo gm is working in (the checkout the tool runs from, root). It no longer reads or checks fx, thebird, jayzee, hy4-relay or hyperagent, and no peer path appears in the code or the skill.
- Code: native/components/tool/repos.cpp takes the root (repos_command(root, strict)); native/include/gm/tool.hpp and native/components/tool/main.cpp pass it. Report mode exits 0; --strict exits 1 when the root repo has uncommitted files or commits ahead of origin, or has no upstream.
- Phase B: the Phase B step reports the root repo's state through repos --strict and does not commit unlisted paths. Committing every uncommitted file in a repo would sweep in changes gm did not make, so the commit stays explicit (ship with listed paths) and the push stays in ship --push after Phase B.
- Skill: skills/dev/SKILL.md's end-of-stretch rule names the cwd repo only.

## Round job_status wait in one run_code body (2026-11-12)

- Cause: job_status with a job name clamped waitMs to a fixed job_wait_ceiling_ms of 60000 (native/components/verbs/job.cpp), whatever the job's own timeout. A caller asking for a longer wait got a "running" reply at 60 s and had to call again, so each long wait cost several turns. The body itself was not the cutoff: run_code keeps its foreground until its timeoutMs (default 100000 ms), and the MCP client backgrounds a call still running at 120 s, so a wait longer than the body's timeoutMs still needs the caller to raise timeoutMs.
- Change: job_status with a job name clamps waitMs to the job's own timeout (Job::timeout_ms, which is already capped at the job lifetime) plus the existing 250 ms ended-event grace, instead of the fixed 60 s. The job is killed at its deadline, so the wait ends when the job settles. The pid wait (wait_for_pid, max_wait_ms) is unchanged.
- Witness, new check check-job-wait (native/components/tool/checks/job_wait.cpp, registered in registry.cpp, declared in tool.hpp, listed in CMakeLists.txt): a 65 s job waited on with waitMs 120000 inside one run_code body returns state exited after 65008 ms, not backgrounded. The old 60 s ceiling would return running at 60 s and fail it.
- Witness, 300 s wait in one body (run once against the release build, outside Phase B: a 300 s job, job_status waitMs 300000, body timeoutMs 400000): the body returned foreground (ok true) with waitedMs 300001 and state running, because sleep 300 outlasts the 300 s wait by its start-up time. The wait returned at the requested 300 s in one body; the job's exit needs a waitMs that covers the job's duration.
- Regressions on the release build: check-turn-economy, check-job-status-cancel and check-cancel-wait pass.

## Round arm-diagnose dispatch concurrency (2026-11-12)

- Cause: the concurrency group was arm-diagnose-<ref> for every event. On main, cancel-in-progress is false, so a queued workflow_dispatch run was replaced when a newer push queued in the same group. Runs 43166024906 and 43166694461 were cancelled with no jobs that way.

- Local witness: the YAML parses, and the group expression resolves per event: for workflow_dispatch the group carries the run id (unique per run), and for push it carries the ref (the same group as before).

## Round ASan per-call retention: cause from the live heap (2026-11-12)

- Change: an ASan-only probe (native/components/host/asan_probe.cpp, installed by run_worker only when GMNEW_ASAN_PROBE=1 and only in a build compiled with AddressSanitizer). On SIGUSR2 the worker writes "asan-heap live <bytes> heap <bytes>" to stderr from __sanitizer_get_current_allocated_bytes and __sanitizer_get_heap_size. The release build compiles the probe to a no-op.
- Check: check-asan-retention (native/components/tool/checks/asan_retention.cpp, registered) reads the live heap after 100 warm calls and after each 400-call window. It is skipped unless GMNEW_ASAN_PROBE=1, so Phase B on the release build does not run it.
- Witness, build/asan, GMNEW_ASAN_PROBE=1, quarantine_size_mb=0, wall 71 s: "check-asan-retention: ok (live heap per run_code call over the second 400 calls: 9.800000 bytes (live 441688 after warm-up, 689577 then 693497 bytes))".
- Cause: the live heap grows about 10 bytes per call in the second window, so the earlier 8.5 KB per call was not live objects. It is allocator metadata and resident memory that ASan keeps (heap size minus live bytes), not retained state. LeakSanitizer was already clean at exit (an earlier round). The release build shows no per-call growth over 4000 calls. Item closed: no product change is needed for it.

## Round owner decisions taken in Phase A (2026-11-12)

Decided here by the worker, with the reason, so the owner can overturn any of them.

- ASan job policy: the asan-arm job keeps memory-safety checks plus the checks that pass hosted. The seven timing checks stay out of the asan default until their hosted run passes. Reason: a timing check under ASan measures the sanitizer's slowdown, not the product.
- Protocol 2026-07-28 capability flag: stays unimplemented. Reason: no client we connect to advertises it, and both engines negotiate only the 2025 versions, so a flag with no caller adds code with no witness.
- next_context cancel behaviour: unchanged. The relay stops resending a cancelled next_context, and the wait runs to its own bound. Reason: the bound already limits the wait, and a resend on cancel would replay events the client already received.
- Shared rules text: unchanged. Re-reading the rules at every step is the design (AGENTS.md, "gm: agent instructions"). Reason: the rules are short and the re-read is what keeps a long run on them.

Scenario 2: the gate SIGKILLed with a page open, and the next call reaches the page without ECONNREFUSED. ## Round playwriter scenario 2: cause (2026-11-12, Phase A)

- Witness: check-browser-first-open scenario 2 fails at pw f26b5ce with "WITNESS open=false pages=[] contexts=[1,1,0] executorIndex=2". Scenarios 1 (open, wait, check, close) and 3 (PLAYWRITER_BROWSER_PATH) pass.
- Chrome-side listing, raw CDP (Target.getBrowserContexts and Target.getTargets) in the same gm flow, fresh sandbox at f26b5ce:
  - after the first open: nonDefaultContexts=[0D1E..., 3FC9...]; pages: about:blank in the default context 021C..., about:blank in 3FC9..., and the caller's page http://127.0.0.1:19838/ in 0D1E... (a non-default context).
  - after the gate SIGKILL, before the next call: nonDefaultContexts=[]; pages=[about:blank in the default context 021C...]. The caller's page and both non-default contexts are gone.
- Control, outside gm: a Playwright client against a headless Chromium on its own port. Client A does newContext(), opens a page on a local URL, and is SIGKILLed. Client B, 2 s later, lists only about:blank in the default context. Client A's page opened in the default context (browser.contexts()[0]) survives the same kill.
- Source of the mechanism: the sandbox copy of @xmorse/playwright-core, lib/server/chromium/crBrowser.js (doCreateNewContext), sends Target.createBrowserContext with disposeOnDetach: true. Chrome disposes such a context, and its pages, when the connection that created it closes.
- Why the gm flow loses the page: the gate SIGKILL retires the proxy's child (the executor), which closes the executor's CDP connection. Chrome disposes the non-default contexts that connection created. The next call starts a new executor, which has no pages (CHECK above).
- Not traced: which call in the executor or in connectOverCDP creates the non-default context that the caller's page lands in. executor.js takes contexts[0] when browser.contexts() is non-empty, and an earlier shim log showed one context with one page at connect, so the cause is not fully explained. This is open for the playwriter peer, who owns the fix.
- Consequence: a gm-side change cannot keep the page. The page must be created in a context that outlives the executor's connection (the default context, or a context without disposeOnDetach). The owner's requirement that an opened page stays open is the criterion for the peer's change.

## Round playwriter turn-end lease signal: design (2026-11-12, Phase A)

- Problem: the playwriter lease is the MCP connection that gm's StdioClient holds to the gate launcher. The client lives in McpVerbs, which run_worker owns (native/components/host/worker.cpp, mcpclient::McpVerbs at line 151). It is released only when the worker stops, so it spans the caller's turns. Nothing in gm sees a turn boundary today.
- Signals considered:
  - next_context wait: it runs while the turn is still going, so it marks a wait, not an end.
  - finish: it ends the run, and a run spans many turns.
  - MCP connection close: it happens at worker stop, not at turn end.
  - Gate idle timer (300 s in the launcher): it is elapsed time, so it can drop a lease in the middle of a turn or hold one for 5 minutes after the turn ends. It stays as the backstop.
  - Claude Code Stop hook (chosen): it fires when the main agent ends a response. The bundled CLI on this host names the Stop and SubagentStop hook events, and its hook input carries stop_hook_active. The evidence is a string search of the bundled CLI, not a hook run. The first implementation run must confirm the payload fields (session_id, cwd).
- Hook entry: /config/.claude/settings.json already has a "hooks" object (a PreToolUse entry runs rtk). A Stop entry takes the same shape: "Stop": [{"hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "<gm turn-end command>"}]}]. Stop has no matcher.
- Hook command: reads the hook JSON from stdin and writes a marker under the gm state directory (turn-end/<key>.json with cwd, session_id and the time in ms). It writes to a temp file and renames it, so a reader never sees a partial file, then exits 0 at once. It makes no network call and returns no decision, so it cannot keep the turn running, including when stop_hook_active is true.
- Key: the workspace (cwd), since one worker serves one workspace. Two sessions in one workspace share the marker. One session's turn end then releases the other's lease; the lazy reconnect recovers, but the page is lost unless the pw change below is in place (owner decision 2).
- Worker side: a release thread owned by McpVerbs, woken every 5 s. It must not be the MCP monitor thread. mcp::Server's monitor_loop (native/components/mcp/server.cpp, about line 1904) returns when no body or shell job is open and restarts only on demand, so it cannot run an unconditional tick. Each tick, for each playwriter client that holds a lease: if the marker time is later than the client's last call start and no call is in flight, call StdioClient::release().
- StdioClient::release(): close the child's stdin (the launcher's proxy sees EOF and drops the lease), call lose() with the reason "released at the end of the caller's turn", and leave core_->closing unset. stop() sets closing and connect() refuses while it is set (native/components/mcpclient/client.cpp, the accepted check near line 265), so release must not call stop(). The next call_tool reconnects through the lazy path (native/components/mcpclient/mcpclient.cpp, lazy start near lines 187-194).
- Race: a call can start between the marker check and the release. release takes the client's call lock, re-checks that the last call started before the marker, and refuses when a call is in flight.
- Expected: the gate and browser stay up; only the lease ends. Not yet observed. The witness below must show it.
- Dependency: release must not ship before the playwriter peer's change that keeps an opened page across the executor connection (see the cause section above). Today a release at turn end drops the caller's page at the next turn, which is the scenario 2 failure in normal use. So the release waits for the pin move (kPlaywriterPin in native/components/host/install.cpp, and the marker in lazy_browser.cpp).
- Witness plan (check-turn-end-release, a new check; not written in this round):
  1. Sandbox install at the pin; gm serve; playwriter_execute opens a page on a local URL and waits 2 s.
  2. Run the hook command with stdin {"session_id":"t1","cwd":"<workspace>"}.
  3. Poll the status JSON of playwriter-project for up to 10 s until its lease count is 0. Print WITNESS released=<count> gate=<pid> browser=<pid>. The field name is to be checked against pw's status output at implementation.
  4. The next playwriter_execute reads the page URL. It must still be the local URL after the pw change. Print WITNESS page=<url>.
  5. Stop the sandbox and check for survivors, as check_lazy_browser does.
- Owner decisions:
  1. Writing a Stop entry into /config/.claude/settings.json changes the user's Claude settings outside the checkout. Recommendation: gm install adds it only with the owner's yes; otherwise the owner adds the entry by hand.
  2. Key: workspace (recommended) or session_id. The workspace matches one worker per workspace. Session keying needs the session id to reach the worker, which it does not have today.
  3. Timing: implement after the peer's pw change lands and the pin moves, not now. Recommendation: after.
- This round: design only. No code, hook, settings or pw change was made.

### Item 1: skill serving and the run_code wait

- c2ec399 (the refusal and the skill read). Witness: check no-resource-client, through the viaVerb case of 6d6effc, which compares the body's read with the size of the file (17297 bytes today). Not run.
- 28266e7 (the foreground cap). The foreground wait of run_code is capped at 100000 ms (kForegroundCapMs, scaled by clock_scale), so a body still running at the cap becomes a background run before the client's 120 s limit. A larger timeoutMs is accepted and held to the cap; the schema still allows up to 3600000. Witness: check run-code-budget, new case "foreground cap": a body that spins scaled(115000) ms at timeoutMs 300000 must return with background set, after at least scaled(95000) ms and before scaled(115000) ms. The skill now says a body still running at 100 seconds becomes a background run, whose value comes from job_status with its job id, and that a gm.read_file of a skill:// file is returned whole. AGENTS.md records the cap in place of the 150 s fact of 2026-11-08. Witness: read against the code. The gate (gm-tool gate, agents-size) has not run.

A host that cannot read resources (fx) keeps working. A host that does not read the skill gets no rules from the refusal. Keeping the pass-through, or requiring a read that is recorded, is the owner's call.

### Item 2: turn-end lease (code only, release gated off)

- 9a35aa1 (StdioClient::release and the release tick). StdioClient::release(ended_ms) takes the use lock exclusively with try_lock, so it skips a client with a call in flight. It skips a client whose last use (call or connect) is after the turn's end time. Otherwise it closes stdin through lose(), with the reason "released at the end of the caller's turn", waits up to 5 s for the launcher to exit, and kills it if it has not. It does not set core_->closing, so the next call reconnects through connect(true). McpVerbs runs a release tick every 5 s only when Options.release_at_turn_end is set, and it releases only lazy servers (the playwriter entry is lazy). Off by default. Witness: check-turn-end-release, to be written; not run.
- 82dfa2c (the hook, the marker and the flag). gm turn-end reads the Stop hook JSON from stdin, takes cwd and session_id, and writes $HOME/.gmnew/turn-end/<hash of the canonical workspace>.json with workspace, session_id and ended_ms, through a temp file and a rename. It exits 0 in every case. The worker reads the marker through turn_ended_ms, and gm serve forwards --release-at-turn-end yes to the worker (relay.cpp, serve.cpp, worker.cpp). gm install prints the Stop entry and leaves the Claude settings file unchanged (register_installed, print_turn_end_hook). Witness: not run. check-turn-end-release must start gm serve with the flag, run a playwriter call, run the hook with the workspace in its JSON, and confirm the lease count drops and the page is still there after the next call.
- Gate: the release stays off until pw's page-survival commit lands and the pin moves. Release before that commit drops the caller's page at the turn end, which is scenario 2 in normal use. Do not pass --release-at-turn-end yes in the gm MCP entry until that commit is pinned.
- Not verified on this host: that the Stop hook input carries cwd and session_id. The marker falls back to the process's current directory when cwd is absent. The first run of the hook confirms the fields.
- Decision for the owner: whether gm install may write the Stop entry into the Claude settings file. This round does not write it; the entry is printed.
- Decision for the owner: whether the flag belongs in the gm MCP entry, which the install writes. This round does not change that entry.

## Round 2026-11-13 (queue e6b5, Phase A): update order by commit time

- Scope: a local build decides whether to take a published build by commit time when both carry one. A build with no commit time to compare (serial 1 or no numeric serial) refuses a published build it cannot order, instead of taking it.
- Commit A: the commit time in the build (cmake/gmnew_stamp.cmake writes kBuildCommitTime; native/components/host/main.cpp prints it after the commit id in --version); ManifestAsset and UpdatePolicy carry committed (native/components/host/include/gm/host/update.hpp); order_against in native/components/host/update.cpp decides Newer, Older or Unordered; native/components/tool/release.cpp writes committed into each asset; native/components/tool/checks/update_order.cpp is the check; AGENTS.md states the rule.
- Witness: gm-tool check build/release/native/components/host/gm check-update-order, on a serial-1 build with a commit time. Four legs: a published commit older than the build's is kept; an equal and a newer commit are taken; a published asset with no commit time is refused. Before the commit: ok, all four legs (0.32 s wall).
- Red control: the serial-only ordering of 3971b52 took serial 14 over 15 (AGENTS.md, the update order note as committed in 3971b52).
- Not claimed: a published asset from before this change has no committed field, so a serial-1 build refuses it until a CI publish writes committed.
- Commit B: a relay holds a re-exec while a background body job runs. native/components/mcp/server.cpp publish_bodies sends gm/bodies with the running count when a background body starts and when any body ends; the count is computed and sent under one lock, so the last count the relay gets is current. native/components/host/relay.cpp takes gm/bodies (never forwarded to the host), holds reexec while bodies_running_ is above 0 and says once that it waits; native/components/host/include/gm/host/relay.hpp carries the count. relay.cpp also says the update's kept and refused status (commit A). native/components/tool/checks/body_reexec.cpp is the check; it is registered in registry.cpp and declared in native/include/gm/tool.hpp, and built through native/components/tool/CMakeLists.txt.
- Witness needed: gm-tool check build/release/native/components/host/gm check-body-reexec. A background body (run_shell sleep 5) runs; the install pointer moves to a second build during it. The relay must say it waits for 1 running body job, must not re-exec during a 1 s hold, the in-flight job_status must answer with the body's value, the relay must re-exec after the body ends, and the worker must run from the second build. Not run when this commit was made; the result is recorded with Phase B.
- Commit C: the two relay checks offer a version a CI serial cannot pass, and phase-b fails a skipped gating row. native/components/tool/checks/relay_reexec.cpp offers ffff111-9999999999 with committed 4102444800 in place of ffff111-99, and its updated marker follows the offer; native/components/tool/checks/handover_in_flight.cpp offers ffff222-9999999999 with the same commit time; native/components/tool/driver.cpp fails a row whose output reads "ok (skipped (" unless the skip is for a platform ("not on this platform"). The two relay checks skip on a dev stamp, so a set built on a dev stamp now fails them instead of passing them.
- Witness needed: phase-b on a CI-shaped build (-DGMNEW_VERSION=<sha>-1). check-relay-reexec and check-handover-in-flight must each report ok with its own summary, not skipped; the set output must contain no "ok (skipped (" row.
- Commit D: check-body-reexec reads the body's value after the hold, in one run_code call that awaits job_status (native/components/tool/checks/body_reexec.cpp). The first version sent job_status as a tools/call before the install pointer moved; the code surface serves no job_status tool, so it answered "Unknown tool" and the call went out before the hold. Now the call goes after the hold, so no call is in flight during the hold and only the body gate holds the re-exec. Witness, on the CI-shaped build 8e21a32-1: ok in 7.6 s wall. The relay said it waits for 1 running body job; it did not re-exec in the 1 s hold; the body answered with its value at 4019 ms; the relay re-executed at 4220 ms; the worker ran the second build at 4274 ms.
- Red control: the same check on a build of ca280d5 (the parent of commit B; git archive into /tmp/gm-red, built in 174 s) fails four ways: no wait marker, a re-exec during the body, the worker ended while the body ran, and the body was killed with no value.

## Round 2026-11-13 (open items after fb9ba): pw first-pass re-exec, update-order red control, clock-mutations reason

- Item 1, the pw relay (308262) did not re-exec on the first pass after the install. Cause: host state, not gm. The install started at 23:35:21Z. At that moment the pw host had a run_code call in flight that waits on gm.job_status (job pb-fullset-p2, waitMs 90000). Its run log (/workspace/pw/runs/2026-11-12-17-54-18-b8bdb4/log.jsonl) has: action run_code at 23:34:47.294Z (seq 3394); code-call job_status at 23:36:17.327Z (seq 3395); result at 23:36:17.388Z (seq 3399); restart build 233d802b8a7c-dev -> 4a82bc9d4b18-dev at 23:36:17.662Z (seq 3401). The host transcript (/config/.claude/projects/-workspace-pw/ad1b4f62-ca69-413b-80fb-cb4a6086499e.jsonl) shows the same call as a tool_use with no result until 23:36:17.
- Why the call held the re-exec: the relay re-executes only while every call in flight is next_context (only_resendable_in_flight in native/components/host/relay.cpp). The watch pass set the pending flag on its first 2 s tick after the pointer moved, and the re-exec then waited for the call. It followed 0.27 s after the answer. That is the designed rule, so an answer is not lost; it is not a defect in the re-exec path.
- Consequence for the owner to decide: an install waits for any call that is not next_context, so a long job_status wait holds it for up to the wait (90 s here, 100 s at most). Whether job_status may be resent to the new worker is the owner's call. Not changed here.
- Evidence gap: the relay writes its say lines to stderr. The pw and gm-workspace MCP logs under /config/.cache/claude-cli-nodejs/ hold only the startup line, so the run log's restart event is the only record of when a relay moved.
- Item 2, the commit-time legs of check-update-order. Before the fix the check, run on the 3971b52 binary, failed at its parse ("the build prints no commit time"), which says nothing about the legs (/tmp/red3971-update-order-before.out). The fix has two parts. The check takes a build's commit time from git when --version prints none, using the commit field. The legs' serials run against commit order (older commit with serial 99, equal and newer with serial 0, no commit time with a non-numeric serial), so a serial-only ordering fails every leg.
- Red control: the 3971b52 host binary, built from git archive 3971b52 in /tmp/gm-red-3971 (the scratch stamp script's commit and head defaults set to 3971b52, because the archive has no .git; gm target only; 205 s from 23:44:31Z to the link at 23:47:56Z). All four legs fail: the older commit is taken (expected kept), the equal and the newer commit are kept as older (expected taken), and the build with no commit time is taken (expected refused). Output: /tmp/red3971-update-order-after.out.
- Green: the current host build 4a82bc9d4b18-dev (commit time 1794526209) gives kept, taken, taken, refused in 0.78 s (/tmp/head-update-order.out).
- Item 4, clock-mutations. It stays out of the default set. The reason is corrected in the next round (2026-11-13, finish the push, Item 3): the first wording, "changes the clock every peer shares", was wrong.
- Item 3, this entry and the AGENTS.md notes are committed locally and not pushed. They go out with the next Phase B push.

## Round 2026-11-13 (finish the push): browser scope under load, kill identity, clock-mutations wording

- Item 1, check-browser-scope under load. Four failing runs, each on a different assertion. Loaded run 1 (/tmp/pb2-load-1.out): the second run's open did not list its page, so the peer assertions that follow read a page that was never opened (finish closed 0 pages; "finish closed the second run's page"), and the cleanup side count failed (its value was not printed). Loaded run 2 (/tmp/pb2-load-2.out): the cleanup side count failed, then "a run's page is still open" at cleanup. Loaded run 3 (/tmp/pb2-load-3.out) and the full set (/tmp/phase-b2-full.log, load 17.0 on 16 cores): the cleanup side count was the only failure.
- What the failing reads were. The first cleanup count (sides, after undo) failed in all three later loaded runs with count -1, not with a page left open. Its reply is an executor error: "browserContext.newPage: Target page, context or browser has been closed" at .playwriter-eval.js:1:383, which is the newPage in the browser wrapper's page recovery (kOpenRunContext, native/components/host/browser_scope.cpp): the wrapper runs before every playwriter_execute and calls home.newPage() when state.gmPage is closed or unset. returned() reads -1 for any reply without a return line, so the old message "still open" was wrong for these runs. The earlier loaded failures (before the message printed the count) took the same path, but their replies were cut from the message and are not verified.
- Why each run took a different assertion (loaded runs 1 to 3 of the first set): the cleanup count was one step; the peer's open was another. Under host CPU load (14 busy loops on a 16-core host already at load 4 to 17) Chrome refused or closed targets: "Failed to open a new tab (Target.createTarget)", "Target page ... has been closed", and "Page closed (url: about:blank) for state.gmScopeCheck" with no close from the check. Which call first hit one of these set the assertion that failed. Not a memory limit: memory pressure was 0 and about 9 GB was available; CPU pressure was high.
- Variants tried and not kept. (a) Bounded waits for zero on the cleanup counts: a wait repeats the same executor error, so it adds about 10 s and does not change the result. The waits stay, because they are correct for a count that is still falling. (b) Leaving state.gmPage on a page the undo does not close: the error still came from the recovery. (c) Closing the side pages but not the side context: the error changed shape ("Failed to open a new tab") and the loaded runs still failed. None of these is a fix; the check is still load-sensitive.
- The cleanup messages print the count and the reply they read. The old message "after the browser was closed" was wrong: the counts are read before browser_close_machine in the same run_code.
- Item 2, kill identity. check_browser_scope took its kill roots from processes_mentioning(home), so a process whose command line held the home path, including a foreign one, joined the tree and was killed with no pid or start-time check. Now serve_tree(session) records the session's descendants with their start times before the session stops (owned_of), and stop_owned kills only the entries whose start time still matches the recorded one, then polls up to 3 s for them to exit. The home-path search is no longer a root.
- Witness: check-browser-scope-identity (native/components/tool/checks/browser_scope.cpp). It starts a real gm serve, records its tree through serve_tree, starts a foreign sh whose command line holds the home path (the witness asserts that processes_mentioning finds it, so the old search would have taken it), and starts a sleep whose recorded start time is off by one. After the stop, the serve's processes must be gone, and the foreign process and the mismatched pid must still be alive.
- Item 3, clock-mutations wording. The driver's skip message and the earlier Item 4 note said it "changes the clock every peer shares". The code does not write the host clock. clock_mutations.cpp runs its own gm serve with GM_CLOCK_SCALE=0.0167 (the scale applies only to that serve), rewrites two sources in the shared checkout (native/components/mcp/include/gm/mcp.hpp and native/components/verbs/job.cpp), rebuilds the build tree, and restores each file with its mtime. It stays out of the default set because it edits the shared checkout: a peer that builds during the window compiles a mutant. The default is unchanged; GM_CHECK_MUTATIONS=1 runs it.
- Phase B results are not recorded in this file, because a commit after the Phase B pass would move HEAD past the marker that gm-tool ship --push checks. They are in the report of the round and in the Phase B logs.

## Round 2026-11-13 (fix the browser wrapper under load): recovery, cleanup reads, digest ordering

- Item 1, the browser wrapper (native/components/host/browser_scope.cpp, kOpenRunContext). Before: the home context was browser.contexts()[0] with no fallback, and a closed state page was replaced by one home.newPage() call, so one refused or closed target failed the whole call. The loaded runs of the last round hit "browserContext.newPage: Target page, context or browser has been closed" at that recovery line, and "Failed to open a new tab (Target.createTarget)". After: live() tries each listed context in order and reuses its first open page or opens one. gmNewPage() gives the run's own context.newPage() the same recovery, trying the run's home context first. Both retry up to 5 rounds with backoff 200 ms doubling (sleeps of 200, 400, 800, 1600 and 3200 ms, 6.2 s in all) and then return the last error. The run view is rebuilt when the home context changes (state.gmRunFor); the owned-page set is kept. Bound: 5 rounds over the contexts listed, each newPage bounded by the run's Playwright timeout (60 s).
- Witness, Phase B: check-browser-scope under 14 bounded busy loops, three runs, must pass 3 of 3. Red control: the pre-fix wrapper (the build of ddc3739, kept as /tmp/gm-prefix-bin/gm) under the same loads, with its output quoted in the report.
- Item 2, the count reads of check-browser-scope (native/components/tool/checks/browser_scope.cpp). The three cleanup counts (side pages, the run's page, the peer's page) no longer wait for zero: the waits added in the last round are dropped, because the failing reads were errors from the wrapper's page recovery, which Item 1 now retries, and no run showed a count that a close had not yet settled. Two waits that were in the check before that round stay (the post-finish read of the run's page and the after-peer read of the peer's page): no run here showed they are unneeded either. Every count reply is now checked for ok before its value: a count call that errored is reported as "did not run", with its reply, instead of as an open page. The post-finish and after-peer counts use the same split. Witness: check-browser-scope alone and under load (Phase B); the messages name the failing call.
- Item 3, the update-order fallback (native/components/tool/checks/update_order.cpp). A build's --version prints "<stamp> (<id>) <time>". The id is a tree digest from cmake/gmnew_stamp.cmake (it hashes HEAD:native and HEAD:defaults), not a git commit. The fallback ran git log on that id and reported "git has none for its commit" without naming the cause. Now commit_time_of asks git whether the id is a commit before it reads a time, and a build with no printed time and an id git does not know is refused with the cause: "the update order cannot be checked: the build prints '<id>', which git does not know as a commit in this checkout (a tree digest prints this way), and no commit time". A build that prints a time is ordered by that time, whatever its id.
- Witnesses, Phase B, check-update-order run on: (a) the current build, which prints a digest and a time (9ed4793-1 (30bd342b9554) 1794529759), ordered by its printed time; (b) a build that prints a commit: the current tree built in a scratch copy with the stamp's id set to the git short head, printing "<stamp> (<commit>) <time>"; (c) a stub that prints a digest and no time, which must be refused with the cause. The binary alone cannot map a digest to its commit, so a build with no printed time and a digest is refused. Printing the git short head in the stamp would make the fallback useful for such builds; that is a product change not made here.
- Item 1, addendum: live() and gmNewPage() now open a fresh context (browser.newContext(), closed again when its newPage fails) when every listed context refuses a page. Within the same five attempts and backoff, so the wrapper stays bounded. The loaded run after the first wrapper fix still failed: the sides count hit live()'s final throw with the listed contexts all closed, and the client lists a context only until its close event. Witness: the Phase B rows named in Item 1 above; the results are in the report, not in this file.
- Item 1, addendum 2: the stale browser behind the loaded failures that addendum 1 left. The gate stops Chrome when no lease is held and no caller page is open for GRACE_MS (5 s, pw/bin/playwriter-project). The executor keeps the dead browser object: pw's executor.js ensureConnection checks isConnected only in headless mode. The next call's recovery then fails with "browser has been closed". Diagnosis: a scratch build that put connected, the context list and the gate status into the error showed connected false, an empty context list, and the gate's status line "browser stopped", with a new browser pid for the next call; that scratch edit was reverted. The wrapper now throws gm-browser-gone-before-body when browser.isConnected() is false at entry, and when live() finds no usable page. Both throws come before the body. The host (user_execute, native/components/host/browser_scope.cpp) resends a reply that carries that marker up to five times, with backoff 500, 1000, 2000 and 4000 ms; any other reply is returned unchanged, and a body that already ran is never resent. A pw defect remains and is not changed here: ensureConnection should check isConnected in both modes. Witness: the Phase B rows, with results in the report, not in this file.
- Item 1, addendum 3: the side-page open assertion of check-browser-scope now prints the side reply. Loaded run 3 on eb835d0-1 failed with "the side pages did not open" and no reply, then "side pages are still open after undo: count 1" (the side code creates its other context and page before it sets state.gmSideCheck, so undo cannot close them). The side code takes its project context from browser.contexts()[0] with no fallback, which is the pattern the wrapper stopped using; the next step depends on the reply this change prints. Witness: the Phase B rows, with results in the report, not in this file.

## Round 2026-11-13 (own-browser count: match the words of the command line)
- Cause of the 0 count. own_browsers found the run's main Chromium by its profile path (processes_mentioning), and proc::command_of returned one element for it, not one per argument. Chromium's main process rewrites its argv in place with spaces (set_process_title_linux), so /proc/<pid>/cmdline has no NUL between arguments. main_browser_of compared whole elements with "--user-data-dir=<profile>", which never matched. Diagnostic run (since reverted): processes_mentioning returned the main pid and its zygote, gpu and renderer children, each with one element.
- Fix. main_browser_of joins the command's elements with spaces and reads whitespace-separated words, so a NUL-separated command and a space-separated one match alike. The --type= exclusion and the exact --user-data-dir match are unchanged, so a child process (it carries --type=) and a browser with another profile do not count. The failure text now says "the run's own browser process is not running before close" in place of "is not in its serve tree", which the previous round had left stale.
- Witness, Phase B: the red control (a foreign Chromium on a different profile, counted by the status block and not by the fixed check), then the alone and loaded rows, with the reported own-browser pids and the gate log path of any failing run. Results are in the report, not in this file.

## Round 2026-11-13 (job cap: a job that writes keeps running; Phase A)
- Cause. Index job zero-glb-keep12r3 (run 2026-11-12-18-34-39-628309, pid 2007132, timeoutMs 3600000) was killed at 01:58:41Z with reason timeout after 3600000 ms while it still wrote: its kill tail reads "1847/30944 ok", so it was progressing when the deadline fired. watch() in native/components/verbs/job.cpp used a fixed deadline (min of timeoutMs and the lifetime) and never read the output file or the progress file. The job was relaunched as zero-glb-keep12r4 (pid 2285827) under the same limit.
- Change. job_start takes extendOnProgress: true, an opt-in per job, default false, so every existing job keeps its fixed deadline and lifetime. For such a job timeoutMs is a quiet window: the job is killed only when its output file, and its progress file if one was given, have not been written for timeoutMs, and the job lifetime does not apply. A quiet kill has reason idle, the statement "no output and no progress file change for N ms", and timedOut true. The flag is written to the job status file, so a job adopted after a worker restart keeps it (adopt_job). watch() and snapshot() share progress_time().
- Why opt-in. A job that prints forever would never end under a default. The caller chooses the behavior per job, and job_stop still ends it.
- Files: native/components/verbs/job.cpp, native/components/verbs/core_internal.hpp, native/components/verbs/verbs.cpp (job_start schema and description), native/include/gm/job_text.hpp (the idle statement).
- Witness it needs, Phase B, on the built binary in a scratch workspace (read the output, then delete the scratch):
  W1, progress extends: job_start with extendOnProgress true, timeoutMs 2000, a command that prints one line every 500 ms for 5 s. job_status with waitMs 60000 must give state exited, exitCode 0, and an elapsed time of about 5 s, with no kill.
  W2, the fixed deadline is unchanged: the same command without extendOnProgress and timeoutMs 2000 must end killed with reason timeout at about 2000 ms.
  W3, silence still ends it: extendOnProgress true, timeoutMs 2000, a silent sleep of 30 s. It must end killed with reason idle at about 2000 ms, and its statement must name the quiet window.
  W4, existing bounds: gm-tool phase-b (full set) keeps check-job-bounds (the lifetime path), check-job-wait and check-restart-jobs green.
- Not in this stretch: installing this build, and relaunching the index compaction with extendOnProgress true. The index run must pass extendOnProgress: true on any long job it starts after the install.

## Round 2026-11-13 (job cap, Phase B on a21f8de: a correction to W1 and a limit found)
- W1 as written in the entry above is wrong about job_status. Its wait is clamped to the job's timeoutMs plus the ended-event grace (native/components/verbs/job.cpp, the clamp of requested_ms in status). For a job started with extendOnProgress, timeoutMs is a quiet window, so one job_status call returns state running after about the window while the job still runs. W1 is therefore a loop: job_status until the state is not running, with the calls counted.
- Limit, not changed in this round: a caller of an extendOnProgress job must loop job_status until the state is not running. Next stretch: clamp the wait of an extended job by the verb's wait cap rather than by timeoutMs.

## Round 2026-11-13 (gate-tree stop: Phase A; pushed at af027a4)
- Change, native/components/tool/checks/browser_scope.cpp. This implements the plan in the 2026-11-13 entry above. roots_under finds, in the check's sandbox, each playwriter-project --gate whose PLAYWRITER_PROJECT_DIR is under the sandbox (the environment is read only for a gate command) and each Chromium whose --user-data-dir is under it. run_tree takes those roots through process_tree and keeps each pid with its start time (owned_of), and drops every pid that an owner file names. owner_pids reads the first field of /workspace/*/runs/*/owner and keeps the pids that are alive. stop_run_tree stops what run_tree returns, by pid and start time (stop_owned).
- check_browser_scope. After the serve tree is stopped, the run tree is stopped too, and survivors are a failure. The summary gives the count found before the stop.
- New check check-browser-scope-tree (check_browser_scope_tree; registered in native/components/tool/checks/registry.cpp, declared in native/include/gm/tool.hpp). It installs into its own sandbox HOME, then starts three gates with the installed launcher's start, each in its own workspace under the sandbox. red is the control: it runs no stop and requires exactly one gate in its tree, all of it alive. green requires exactly one gate, runs stop_run_tree, then requires no survivor and an empty tree. guarded names every pid of its tree as an owner, requires an empty stop set, runs the stop, and requires every pid still alive. The fix read only the task event, and it missed a fresh run, whose task is written to task.json by open_run and has no task event. The witness showed the miss, and a second commit (05ddb4d) fixed it and was rebuilt. Cause: the writers of the state the change reads were not all traced before the first build. Rule for the next stretch: before any build in Phase A, list every field the change reads and grep each writer of that field (open_run, task_set, successor creation, the task event). Phase A ends at a commit and a stop. The build and the witness run start in Phase B, and a witness is never used to find out whether Phase A is finished.
- first_step_correction decision. Rule: a corrected task from a connection's first step, meaning the current task is empty or one word and steps is 0, is accepted without owner:true only when all of these hold: the run was created by this connection (open_run made it, not boot reopening an existing run, and not a successor adopted from another connection); no child and no owner has been seen; and the corrected task begins with the current task and continues it. Every other change to a run's task needs owner:true. Reason: the host cuts a slash-command task to its first word on the first call of the connection that opened the run, so the correction must extend the text it cut. A run that another connection opened carries that connection's task, so a change to it is a replacement and falls under the owner rule. Not built in this round. Next stretch, Phase A: a session flag set where the run is created (boot, when resumed is false, and the successor path), and a prefix test in next_context's first_step_correction. The witness for it is written in that Phase A and run in Phase B, where a truncated task is extended, a different task is refused without owner:true, and an adopted run with one-word task is refused.
- Committed as 4dfe6f3 and pushed with ab9b391 (origin/main at ab9b391 at the push of 2026-11-13 02:58Z). The earlier wording "not pushed" was stale.

## Round 2026-11-13 (first_step_correction: Phase A, written before any build)
- Fields the change reads, with every writer found by grep of native/components/mcp/server.cpp at 05ddb4d:
  - steps: boot replay (s().steps += 1 for each next_context result in a reopened log) and next_context's act (s().steps += 1).

  - child_seen: child_context only (= true).
  - owner_seen: next_context's act only (= true).
  - task: boot (the --task of a fresh run; the logged or task.json task of a reopened run), the successor path (s().task = task), task_set, child_context's correction, next_context's correction, and the session prompt (only when the task is empty or inherited).
  - created: new in this round. Writers: boot (= !resumed) and the successor path (= true).
- Changes, all in native/components/mcp/server.cpp unless named:
  1. Session: new field created, default false. The rule needs to know whether this connection opened the run.
  2. boot(): fresh->created = !resumed, set before the session is moved in. A run that boot reopened was not created by this connection.
  3. Successor path: fresh->created = true, because open_run made the new run dir in this connection.
  4. next_context: first_step_correction also needs created, and the corrected task must begin with the current task (corrected.compare(0, task.size(), task) == 0). ## Round 2026-11-17 (bevy session: gm MCP server dropped; Phase A, no build, test or witness run)
- Report. In the bevy session 0f054132 the gm server was gone from the session's tool list at 13:51:05 UTC on 2026-11-16 and the agent wrote "the gm MCP server failed to connect" at 21:48:56 without a connect attempt. Read from the host's transcript, the MCP log (~/.cache/claude-cli-nodejs/-workspace-bevy/mcp-logs-gm) and the gm run logs. The session had no launcher or config fault: the entry connected at 09:33:09 in 427 ms ("gm relay: worker running (pid 36856)", gm 0.1.0, protocol 2025-11-25), and the worker answered restarts until 12:37:19. gm uses stdio (`gm serve`, args serve, from the entry install prints); it opens no port and no socket. The only socket in the flow is the playwriter gate port, which is for browser work and is not the gm connection.
- Cause of the drop: not found in the logs. Claude Code logs its own SIGINT ("Sending SIGINT to MCP server process", seen at 07:02:21 for the earlier connection) and logs no stop for the 09:33 connection. The relay printed nothing, because it reports every exit it knows (host closed, worker exited, failed start, re-exec) and it had no handler for SIGTERM, SIGINT or SIGHUP, so a signal ended it silently. At 13:51:05 a background cargo test in the same session was also killed with exit 143, from outside the session's own commands (the transcript has no kill of its own at that time). No install changed the binary between 15:30 and 16:10 local (13:30 to 14:10 UTC), so an install swap is ruled out.
- Change 1, native/components/host/serve.cpp: run_serve installs handlers for SIGTERM, SIGINT and SIGHUP (POSIX). Each writes one line, "gm relay: stopped by SIGTERM" (or SIGINT or SIGHUP), to stderr and exits with 128 plus the signal. Before, the exit was silent. The worker is not changed; check-serve-signal-reason measures whether it ends with the relay. Witness: check-serve-signal-reason (native/components/tool/checks/serve_entry.cpp).
- Change 2, witness that a fresh session connects: check-serve-entry-connects (native/components/tool/checks/serve_entry.cpp). It starts the binary as the install prints the entry (command, args serve, no flags) in a workspace with no harness config, and needs initialize to answer as gm, tools/list to name run_code and next_context, and resources/read of skill://gm/SKILL.md to answer. Witness: this check passes in phase-b on the release tree.
- Change 3, skills/gm/SKILL.md: the bench rule. A wait on a started job's PID is bounded and holds in the same turn, and a Monitor is never used, because a turn that ends under a Monitor loses its wait.
- Phase B: build the release preset, run check-serve-entry-connects and check-serve-signal-reason by name, then phase-b. If check-serve-signal-reason fails on "the worker outlived the relay's SIGTERM", the worker does not end on input EOF alone, and the fix is in the worker, not in this handler.

## Round 2026-11-17 (bevy's gm connection again: relay exit, restart, stale state; Phase A, no build, test or witness run)
- Evidence, read once. bevy session 0f054132 (claude pid 36664, started 2026-11-16 11:33 local = 09:33 UTC) had no gm child at 2026-11-17 01:27 local. Its gm worker (pid 36856) connected at 09:33 and its run log (runs/2026-11-16-09-33-09-79beb8) ends at 12:37 with no paused event. The worker logs paused ("the supervisor ended stdin") when its stdin closes, so a relay that ended normally would have left that line. Both processes ended with no line in any log, at about 13:51 UTC.
- Ruled out by reading the code: (a) no socket or port: stdio only; (b) a stale lock does not block a new serve: the update lock (update.cpp acquire_update_lock) is taken over when its owner pid is gone or it has aged out, and the pending lock is per run dir and ages out (pending.cpp); (c) a new serve gets a new run dir unless --run-dir or --runs names one; (d) the worker's stop_orphans (job.cpp) kills a recorded pid only when pid_is_foreign is false, which needs the pid dead or matched to the job's exit file, so a reused pid that is alive is not signalled; (e) the ledger reap (proc.cpp reap_ledger) requires the recorded start time to match; (f) the owner registry (proc.cpp Enrolment) removes an entry when its child's enrolment ends; (g) no install changed the binary between 15:30 and 16:10 local.
- Not ruled out: an external SIGKILL or a crash of the relay. Both leave no line (the relay has no handler for them), and a group kill that takes relay and worker together would explain the missing paused line. A kernel log (dmesg) is not readable from this session, so an OOM kill or segfault cannot be confirmed.
- Change 1, native/components/host/relay.cpp, relay.hpp: every say() line also goes to RelayOptions::run_log (append_run_log), so the stop reasons land in the run dir's relay.log. Each line is "<epoch ms> <message>".
- Change 2, native/components/host/serve.cpp: run_serve creates the run dir, opens relay.log (O_APPEND, O_CLOEXEC, so the worker and a re-exec do not inherit it) and writes "started <identity>". The stop handler also writes "gm relay: stopped by SIGTERM|SIGINT|SIGHUP" to that file. A start line with no stop line after it means the relay ended without a handled signal or a say() reason: SIGKILL, a crash, or a group kill.
- Change 3, witness check-relay-reconnects (native/components/tool/checks/serve_entry.cpp): serve starts in a run dir, its relay is SIGKILLed, and its worker must end within 8 s; a second serve on the same run dir and workspace must answer initialize as gm, list run_code and read the skill; relay.log must hold two start lines. Phase B also runs the old binary (build/asan at bef07db) against it, which must fail if the reconnect or the worker-cleanup property does not hold there.
- What would settle the cause: the next occurrence. Read the run dir's relay.log. A start line with no stop line and no paused line in the worker log means an unhandled kill of both processes (SIGKILL or a group kill from outside gm); a stop line names the signal; a say() line names the exit path (host closed, worker exited, failed start, re-exec).

## Round 2026-11-17 (arm-diagnose 43975271788, asan-arm): Phase A

- Failure: the asan-arm job of arm-diagnose run 43975271788 (bef07db) failed check-quickjs-baseline with "4 failure(s)": run_code call 38 did not return 1: null; "the worker gave no reply to run_code call 38; its stderr ends: gm relay: worker running (pid 5708)"; calls 39 and 40 did not return 1: null. The gdb-arm job passed.
- Cause (inferred from the log; not measured in Phase A): the check's Session used the default 180 s watchdog (Session::start, watchdog_ms). Its 41 serial run_code calls on the asan build did not all finish in 180 s, so the watchdog killed the relay's process group during call 38. The reply reader closed, rpc returned null, and calls 39 and 40 found the child gone (send fails) and returned null at once. The stderr has no AddressSanitizer report and no restart line, which fits a watchdog kill and not an asan abort or a worker crash.
- Not ruled out: a real stall in call 38 that ran until the watchdog. The log cannot separate the two; the expiry flag below does.
- Change 1, native/components/tool/checks/quickjs_baseline.cpp: the check's Session takes kWatchdogMs = 600000. Change 2, native/components/tool/session.cpp and native/include/gm/tool.hpp: Session::expired() is set when the watchdog fires. The failure now reads "the worker gave no reply to run_code call N (session watchdog expired: yes|no)". Commit afb04a8.
- Witness: gm-tool check on the asan build (env -u LD_PRELOAD) runs check-quickjs-baseline. It passes with the summary's per-call growth and first run_code time. On the bef07db asan build the same check fails with the 180 s budget only if a call takes more than about 4.4 s; the per-call time has not been measured, and Phase B measures it.
- What would settle the cause: a failure line that reads "session watchdog expired: yes" means the budget was too short for the calls; "no" means the worker stopped answering before the budget ran out. The summary's "first run_code ... ms" gives the per-call scale on the asan build.
- Hosted: accd59b's arm-diagnose run 43981360553 failed the same way on asan-arm (check-quickjs-baseline: call 38 null, call 38 stderr ends at "worker running (pid 5714)", calls 39 and 40 null). gdb-arm passed. The same failure in two runs, both at call 38, is the case the expiry flag separates.
- Measured in Phase B on this host (x86_64, not the arm runner): the asan build's check-quickjs-baseline passes in 3.9 s wall for 41 calls (first run_code 110 ms, about 100 ms per call), so a 180 s budget would need about 4.4 s per call on the arm runner, roughly 40 times slower. The budget is therefore an unlikely cause, and the 600 s budget may only delay a real stall.
- Measured in Phase B: a driven gm serve on the asan build holds 5 threads through 40 run_code calls (no thread leak) and its resident memory grows about 7 MB per call (58 MB at rest, 355 MB after 40). The release build stays at about 11 MB and 10 ms per call. The growth is the ASan allocator, not a gm leak; gm sets no memory limit or rlimit.
- Phase B witnesses at 75c550b: release phase-b "checks: 73 run, 0 failed"; the workflow's 36-check asan-arm list on the local asan build (env -u LD_PRELOAD, the CI ASAN_OPTIONS) "ok" for all 36, check-quickjs-baseline included.
- Not settled: the arm runner's failure at call 38. The next arm-diagnose run's check-quickjs-baseline line says "session watchdog expired: yes" (the 600 s budget ran out, so the worker was slow or stalled) or "no" (the worker stopped answering before the budget ran out, a stall or a crash).

Reading the code, neither touches the gate tree: b8865bf is a workflow file and c92f616 changes only check-quickjs-baseline. The check code itself did not change since the last green release, so the failure is not a regression by a changed line.
- Cause, from the code (not reproduced; no local run was allowed): check-browser-scope-tree takes one snapshot of the owner-file control's gate tree, names those pids, and then expects a second snapshot (run_tree with those pids excluded) to be empty. Chromium starts helper processes after the gate reports "browser ready", so a helper that starts between the two snapshots is not named, and it lands in the stop set. The check then fails although no owner-named process was stopped.
- Fix (commit cf797f9, native/components/tool/checks/browser_scope.cpp):
  - settled_tree(sandbox) polls the gate tree every 500 ms until two consecutive snapshots have the same pids (at most 10 s), and the control names the settled set.
  - A failure lists each process in the stop set with its command text (pid and command, 160 chars), so the next failure shows which process it was.
  - The witness is not weakened: the owner-named processes must still stay alive, which the check still asserts (alive_of on the settled tree after stop_owned).
- Not verified: that a helper process starts in that window on the arm64 row. The failure text now names the process if it does not.

## Eighth stretch 2026-11-18 (freddie blocker: package names and exports subpaths in the module loader): Phase A

- Blocker (freddie's report): freddie's agent code imports `@freddie/freddie-runtime/fs-promises`. gm's loader (native/components/quickjs/engine.cpp, load_module_from_disk) read each specifier as a literal path, so a bare package name failed with "could not load module". fx's embedded loader needs the same rule.
- Change 1 (commit a2c8f1e, native/components/quickjs/resolve.cpp new, engine.cpp, engine.hpp, quickjs CMakeLists):
  - resolve_module_path resolves a bare specifier by walking node_modules from the importing directory up to the root. The first node_modules/<package> directory is the package.
  - The package's exports map is read with the import and default conditions: exact subpaths, * patterns (the longest prefix wins), nested condition objects and arrays. main (then main.js, main/index.js, index.js) is used only where exports is absent. A subpath that exports does not list is refused.
  - Relative and absolute specifiers keep their handling: a relative one is joined to the importer's directory and normalized, as QuickJS did. tjs: and node: names pass through unchanged.
  - normalize_module_name is installed as the QuickJS normalizer in both Engine constructors, with the session as opaque. The importer directory is the module file's own directory; for a non-file base such as "<body>" it is the session's workspace. A relative specifier from a non-file base now resolves against the workspace, where before it resolved against the process directory.
  - Not changed: tjs.setImportMap (unused, not the contract); the CommonJS require in runcode.cpp still ignores exports; the package.json imports (#) map is not implemented.
- Change 2 (commit 3381b96, checks/module_exports.cpp new, registry.cpp, tool.hpp, tool CMakeLists): check-module-exports writes node_modules into a sandbox workspace and runs a body that imports, by name, `@acme/pkg` (exports "." with import), `@acme/pkg/sub` (an exact subpath with require before default: default is chosen), `@acme/pkg/feature/alpha` (an exports pattern), `legacy-pkg` (main, no exports), and `@acme/pkg/hidden` (not exported, must be refused). Expected reply: root-import,sub-default,feature-alpha-import,legacy-main,refused. On the old loader the first import fails with "could not load module".
